metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready coaching knowledge for indoor six-player volleyball serving, serve receive, and passing, including serve-type progressions, court zones, targeting, risk management, receive systems, seam rules, platform mechanics, role responsibilities, assessment metrics, common errors, and level-specific teaching implications.

source_refs.title: Official Volleyball Rules 2025-2028
source_refs.notes: Primary legal reference for service execution, service zone, rotation constraints, back-row/libero constraints, and legal playing contacts.

source_refs.title: Official Volleyball Rules
source_refs.notes: Confirms the 2025-2028 rules cycle as the current FIVB edition commissioned by the 39th FIVB World Congress.

source_refs.title: Coaches Manual Level II
source_refs.notes: Used for volleyball physical characteristics, reception time pressure, low receive posture, kinetic-chain serving, ground-support versus airborne skills, and common stress areas.

source_refs.title: Lesson Plans for Teachers and Coaches
source_refs.notes: Supports gamelike, whole-skill, random practice design and progression through serving, forearm passing, and serve-receive combinations.

source_refs.title: Junior High Lesson Plans
source_refs.notes: Used for beginner/intermediate progressions that combine serving, forearm passing, serve receive, scoring, and smaller-sided play.

source_refs.title: You Win with Serve Reception, not Passing
source_refs.notes: Emphasizes reading the server and ball before contact, over-net serve-receive specificity, and avoiding non-transfer wall or pair passing as the main receive stimulus.

source_refs.title: Five Keys to Better Passing
source_refs.notes: Used for platform angle, serve-type recognition, early tracking, and holding the pass angle through contact.

source_refs.title: Five Keys to a Wicked Jump Float Serve
source_refs.notes: Used for jump-float contact quality, flat trajectory, depth deception, tactical variety, and error-rate management.

source_refs.title: Top Ten Serving Secrets
source_refs.notes: Supports hard-flat serving, serving from varied depths behind the end line, practice feedback with serve speed, and the distinction between net errors and long errors.

source_refs.title: How You Can Make a Huge Impact as a Libero
source_refs.notes: Used for libero serve-receive leadership, taking a larger passing area, helping outside hitters, and communicating tactical intentions.

source_refs.title: Opponent Analysis and Scouting Reports
source_refs.notes: Used for serving target plans, passer tendency scouting, serve type by opponent, seam vulnerability, and receive planning by rotation.

source_refs.title: Young Athletes Mini Volleyball Handbook
source_refs.notes: Used for child-friendly underhand serve mechanics, early movement-to-ball tasks, and progressive distances or net heights.

source_refs.title: Predicting Volleyball Serve-Reception
source_refs.notes: High-level jump-float serve-reception study; receiver initial position and movement, especially large backward displacement, were strong influences on pass type and reception efficacy.

source_refs.title: Characteristics of Serve, Reception and Set That Determine the Setting Efficacy in Men's Volleyball
source_refs.organization_or_author: Jara Gonzalez-Silva, Fernandez-Echeverria, Conejero, Moreno, and collaborators
source_refs.notes: World-class men's volleyball analysis; reception efficacy and setting variables determined setting efficacy more than serve variables in the sampled matches.

source_refs.title: Tactical Determinants of Setting Zone in Elite Men's Volleyball
source_refs.organization_or_author: Afonso, Esteves, Araujo, Thomas, and Mesquita
source_refs.notes: Shows serve depth, jump serve, reception zone, receiver, and low reception can push setters into poorer setting zones; supports deep, high-pressure serve targets and libero receive involvement.

source_refs.title: Variables that Predict Serve Efficacy in Elite Men's Volleyball with Different Quality of Opposition Sets
source_refs.organization_or_author: Valhondo, Fernandez-Echeverria, Gonzalez-Silva, Claver, and Moreno
source_refs.notes: Elite men's serving analysis; serve player, reception zone, reception type, and depending on opposition quality serve type or serve zone predicted serve efficacy.

source_refs.title: The Effect of Jump Topspin Serve Speed on Reception Quality in Men's Volleyball
source_refs.notes: Professional men's match analysis found increasing jump-topspin serve speed was associated with lower reception quality, while faster serves also carried more service-error risk.

source_refs.title: Normative Profiles for Serve Speed for the Training of the Serve and Reception in Volleyball
source_refs.notes: Provides serve-speed ranges and serve-type occurrence data useful for calibrating receive training and machine-fed serve speeds by serve type.

source_refs.title: Whose Ball? Seam Responsibilities in Serve Receive and Defense
source_refs.notes: Used only for practical seam-rule framing: teams need explicit, rehearsed seam ownership rules and realistic repetition under serve pressure.

source_refs.title: Planning Effective Serve-Receive Formations for Lower Skill Level Teams
source_refs.notes: Used for the principle that reducing from more passers to fewer passers should be earned by passing efficiency and team effectiveness, not by copying elite formations.

key_concepts.concept: Serving is the only closed start skill in indoor volleyball and should be treated as the first offensive action.
key_concepts.details: A good serve is not merely in-bounds. It applies pressure by reducing the receiver's time, forcing movement, attacking a weak passer, stressing a seam, changing depth, or making the setter leave the ideal setting zone.

key_concepts.concept: The server must initiate play from the service zone and may not fault the end line or court before the service hit or jump takeoff.
key_concepts.details: The legal constraint matters tactically because servers can use the full service-zone width and depth available behind the end line, including deeper starts for hard float or topspin serves when space allows.

key_concepts.concept: Underhand, standing float, jump float, and jump topspin serves sit on a progression of complexity, speed, trajectory, spin, and physical cost.
key_concepts.details: Underhand serving is an entry skill for ball-over-net success. Standing float adds overhead contact, flat trajectory, and target control. Jump float adds higher contact and more pressure with lower complexity than jump topspin. Jump topspin adds approach, toss, jump, spike-like contact, higher velocity, and greater error/load cost.

key_concepts.concept: Zones 1 through 6 provide a common language for serving, receiving, rotation mapping, and scouting.
key_concepts.details: Back-court zones 1, 6, and 5 are common serve endpoints; front-court short serves can be described by zones 2, 3, and 4 or by short right, short middle, and short left. Backend records should store both numeric zone and descriptive target.

key_concepts.concept: Serve targets should be selected from a hierarchy rather than by habit.
key_concepts.details: Common target priorities are weak passer, overloaded outside hitter, passer with poor movement in a specific direction, seam between passers, short zone that disrupts approach, deep zone that increases setter distance, and rotation-specific traffic that makes the setter or hitter transition harder.

key_concepts.concept: Serve pressure must be balanced against service-error cost and match context.
key_concepts.details: The backend should distinguish controlled pressure from reckless serving. A hard serve to a large tactical target may be appropriate when the server's error rate is acceptable; a lower-risk float or larger target may be better after repeated errors, late in a tight set, or when the opponent is already out of system against moderate pressure.

key_concepts.concept: Float serves pressure passers through late movement, low spin, flat trajectory, and depth deception.
key_concepts.details: Standing and jump float serves should prioritize clean middle-of-ball contact, firm hand shape, low net clearance, repeatable toss, and the ability to hit different depths without obvious cues.

key_concepts.concept: Jump topspin serves pressure passers through velocity, topspin drop, short flight time, and spike-like contact.
key_concepts.details: Research in professional men's volleyball associates higher jump-topspin serve speed with lower reception quality, but this serve type also carries higher physical and service-error cost. It belongs later in the progression unless the athlete can control approach, toss, contact, and landing.

key_concepts.concept: Serve receive is the first action of the side-out phase and determines offensive options.
key_concepts.details: Pass quality shapes whether the setter can use middles, tempo, combination play, and full court. A merely playable pass may keep the rally alive; a positive or perfect pass expands first-ball attack choices.

key_concepts.concept: Most serve-receive success begins before contact through reading server cues and ball flight.
key_concepts.details: Passers should identify server type, start position, toss, contact, trajectory, spin or lack of spin, and likely landing depth. Technical platform work should be embedded in real over-net serve reads as early as possible.

key_concepts.concept: A passing platform redirects the incoming serve with a stable angle rather than swinging at the ball.
key_concepts.details: Useful passing mechanics include balanced posture, arms connected before contact when time allows, a firm but not locked platform, shoulders and platform angled toward target, quiet contact, and body control after the ball leaves.

key_concepts.concept: Footwork helps the passer arrive in a body position that makes the desired platform angle easier.
key_concepts.details: Shuffle, drop-step, crossover, split-step, and emergency lateral steps are means to create balance and angle. The goal is not to force every ball to the midline; the goal is to control a playable angle under time and trajectory constraints.

key_concepts.concept: Passers need both midline passing and outside-body angle passing.
key_concepts.details: Beginner teaching can start with getting the body behind the ball, but higher-level serve receive includes balls taken outside the midline, especially against float movement, seams, and hard serves. The backend should not treat outside-body passing as automatically incorrect.

key_concepts.concept: Float and topspin serves demand different receive emphases.
key_concepts.details: Float serves require early visual tracking, patient feet, small late adjustments, and platform stability against unpredictable movement. Topspin serves require depth awareness, stronger posture, earlier read of pace/drop, controlled rebound, and often more respect for speed.

key_concepts.concept: Receive formations are tools for personnel, rotation, and serve type, not fixed ideals.
key_concepts.details: Five- and four-person receive can support beginners by reducing court per passer. Three-person receive is a common team default. Two-person receive becomes viable when a libero and another strong passer can cover larger areas without lowering team pass quality or attacking transition.

key_concepts.concept: Seam ownership should be pre-defined and rehearsed before the serve, then communicated quickly during the play.
key_concepts.details: Teams may use left-person owns, right-person owns, libero-priority, short/deep split, or movement-based seam rules. The key is consistency, role clarity, and practice against real serves into the seam.

key_concepts.concept: The libero is usually the serve-receive stabilizer and communication leader.
key_concepts.details: A high-level libero can pass a larger area, steal balls from weaker passers, control free balls, call seam intentions, and help outside hitters preserve their attacking approach. Legal libero constraints still apply in attack and front-zone setting contexts.

key_concepts.concept: Outside hitters commonly balance receive responsibility with immediate transition to attack.
key_concepts.details: Serving plans often target outside hitters because passing can reduce their approach quality. Receive systems should decide how much court each outside takes based on passer quality, rotation, and offensive value.

key_concepts.concept: Pass quality should be measured as graded offensive access, not simply good or bad.
key_concepts.details: Useful grades include ace/error, overpass or direct opponent advantage, negative pass, playable out-of-system pass, positive pass with multiple options, and perfect pass with full offense. Team metrics should also link pass quality to sideout and first-ball kill percentage.

key_concepts.concept: Large backward displacement before receive is a warning sign for reception quality.
key_concepts.details: High-level serve-reception research on jump-float serves found receiver positioning and movement had major influence on pass type and efficacy. Starting too far forward or misreading depth can force late backward movement and reduce control.

key_concepts.concept: Passing drills transfer best when they include over-net serves, real reading, variable trajectories, and a target linked to offense.
key_concepts.details: Pair passing and wall passing can warm up contact shapes but should not be the main assessment of serve receive. Serve receive should connect to pass-set-hit, pass-set-attack decision, or sideout scoring as soon as athletes can manage it safely.

key_concepts.concept: For youth and beginners, court size, ball type, net height, and serve distance should be adjusted to preserve rallies and real decisions.
key_concepts.details: Reducing constraints can allow athletes to serve, receive, and play three contacts earlier. The progression should gradually restore full-court rules as skill and strength allow.

scale.label: error_or_ace
scale.definition: Receiving team cannot make a legal second contact or gives immediate point.

scale.label: poor_or_negative
scale.definition: Ball remains playable but offense is predictable, emergency, or far from target.

scale.label: positive
scale.definition: Setter has at least two realistic attacking options, though not full offense.

scale.label: perfect
scale.definition: Setter can run intended first-tempo and full offense from ideal or near-ideal target.

scale.label: overpass
scale.definition: Pass crosses too tight or over the net and gives opponent an attack or free scoring chance.

tactical_rules.rule: Set a serve-error ceiling by level, score, and server role.
tactical_rules.application: Beginners may need a high make-rate target before tactics. Intermediate and advanced servers can accept more risk if their serves produce enough aces, negative passes, or lower sideout percentage. Late-set pressure should narrow the target or simplify the serve before it removes all pressure.

tactical_rules.rule: A serve into the net is usually a poorer training and match error than a long aggressive miss.
tactical_rules.application: A net serve gives no read to receivers and no pressure to the opponent. In training, long errors can still help receivers learn out-ball reads, but repeated long errors still require target and contact correction.

tactical_rules.rule: Serve the weakest functional passer in the current rotation, not simply the weakest athlete.
tactical_rules.application: A strong passer can become vulnerable when moving backward, receiving short, passing after an error, or transitioning to hit. A weaker passer may be hidden. Target decisions must use rotation and movement context.

tactical_rules.rule: Avoid serving the elite libero unless the serve plan intentionally exploits libero movement or bait.
tactical_rules.application: High-level liberos often stabilize large court areas. Serving away can expose outsides, opposites, or seams. If the libero overextends, short/deep or behind-libero targets may become available.

tactical_rules.rule: Serving an outside hitter can reduce their approach quality and first-ball attack readiness.
tactical_rules.application: This is most useful when the outside is both a primary passer and a primary attacker. The serve should make the hitter pass, move, or communicate through a seam before transitioning.

tactical_rules.rule: Seam serving should target confusion or movement, not vague middle space.
tactical_rules.application: A good seam serve lands between ownership zones, moves late, or forces two passers to decide under time pressure. The server and staff should know which two passers are being stressed and why.

tactical_rules.rule: Use short and deep serves to change passer starting posture and setter/hitter traffic.
tactical_rules.application: Short serves can pull front-row hitters away from approach lanes or make non-passers handle the ball. Deep serves can increase setter distance, force backward movement, or push the pass target off the net.

tactical_rules.rule: Match target precision to server strength.
tactical_rules.application: Beginner servers target halves or thirds. Intermediate servers target zones and depth bands. Advanced servers target a player-zone-depth combination such as zone 1 deep on an outside's right shoulder.

tactical_rules.rule: Use three-person receive as the default competitive teaching system once passers can cover larger lanes.
tactical_rules.application: Three passers usually give clear lanes while keeping setter and attacker transition manageable. Teams can start with four or five passers and move to three when metrics support it.

tactical_rules.rule: Two-person receive is earned by data and personnel, not copied from elite teams.
tactical_rules.application: Use it when a libero and another passer can cover the court with equal or better pass quality and sideout percentage than the three-person pattern, and when freeing an attacker creates enough offensive value.

tactical_rules.rule: Every receive pattern needs a named seam rule before the serve.
tactical_rules.application: The rule can be left owns, right owns, libero owns, short/deep split, or server-angle based. The exact choice is less important than consistent rehearsal and player understanding.

tactical_rules.rule: If the libero has green light to cross seams, that authority must be declared and limited.
tactical_rules.application: The libero can steal balls from weaker passers or shrink an outside hitter's lane, but teammates must know whether the libero owns all seam balls, only float serves, only short balls, or only a defined zone.

tactical_rules.rule: Against elite pace, a positive controlled pass is often a better objective than forcing a perfect pass.
tactical_rules.application: Hard jump topspin serves can make perfect passing unrealistic. Passers should avoid overpasses and keep the ball in a playable setting corridor, preserving multiple attack options when possible.

tactical_rules.rule: Starting depth changes by serve type, server contact, and previous ball pattern.
tactical_rules.application: Passers generally respect harder or deeper serves with more depth and float-short servers with readiness to move forward. Starting too shallow against jump topspin or deep float can force damaging backward movement.

tactical_rules.rule: Serving and receiving plans should be rotation-specific.
tactical_rules.application: The same opponent may have different passer lanes, setter paths, and hitter transition stress in each rotation. Record serve targets and receive patterns by rotation rather than as one generic plan.

tactical_rules.rule: Serve-receive practice should be scored by the behavior the team wants in matches.
tactical_rules.application: Score pass quality, seam ownership, first-ball sideout, target hit, or consecutive positive passes. Do not rely on unscored pair passing as evidence that receive is improving.

physical_demands.demand: Serving uses a lower-body, trunk, shoulder, arm, and hand kinetic chain.
physical_demands.relevance: Standing float requires ground-supported transfer; jump float and jump topspin add approach, takeoff, airborne control, and landing.

physical_demands.demand: Jump serving adds repeated jumping and landing load on top of overhead volume.
physical_demands.relevance: Advanced serving sessions should count jump-serve attempts separately from standing serves, especially for athletes who also attack and block heavily.

physical_demands.demand: Serve receive happens under severe time pressure.
physical_demands.relevance: FIVB coaching material notes that elite men's jump-serve reception can require action in roughly 0.7 seconds, while research on jump-float reception highlights short ball-flight times and receiver movement constraints.

physical_demands.demand: Passing and reception require repeated low posture, hip and ankle mobility, and trunk stability.
physical_demands.relevance: Low body position improves control but can fatigue legs and low back if volume and posture are not managed.

physical_demands.demand: Passers repeatedly move laterally, diagonally, forward, and backward before contact.
physical_demands.relevance: Reception quality can drop when passers must make large or late displacement, especially backward. Movement training should be tied to serve reads rather than isolated ladder patterns only.

physical_demands.demand: Passers need shoulder, elbow, wrist, and trunk stability to maintain platform shape under ball speed.
physical_demands.relevance: Platform quality depends on controlling the whole body through contact, not arm tension alone.

physical_demands.demand: Serve receive combines visual perception, tactical memory, communication, and motor control.
physical_demands.relevance: Passers must know the scouting plan, identify serve type, honor seam rules, call the ball, and still create a platform angle.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: High serving volume can contribute to shoulder overload, especially with jump topspin or late high-effort sessions.
